name: Sangiovese

lines.s10: Sangiovese is the red of Chianti and Brunello: sour cherry and tomato leaf on bright acidity and a dusty, savoury grip.
lines.s20: Sangiovese is Tuscany's red, the grape behind Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile. It tastes of sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano, with high acidity and a dusty tannin made for the table.
lines.s45: Sangiovese makes Chianti, Brunello and Vino Nobile, though the labels rarely say so. It is the red of Tuscany, grown on the hills from Florence south to Montalcino. In the glass it is sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano, usually medium in body, with high acidity and a dusty, drying tannin. Brunello is Sangiovese alone, aged at least two years in oak, while Chianti Classico must be at least four fifths Sangiovese. It wants food: pasta in a meat ragù, a grilled steak or aged pecorino. DNA work suggests its parents are Ciliegiolo, still grown in Tuscany, and an almost lost vine found near Naples.
lines.sale: Sangiovese is the red that makes a tomato sauce taste right, its sour cherry and lively acidity meeting the tomato head on. With the pasta or the grilled steak, a Chianti Classico is the bottle I would open.

glass.lead: Sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano on a medium body, with high acidity and a dusty, drying tannin.

ladder.where: The hills of Chianti Classico, Rufina and Montalcino
The Maremma coast at Scansano, and McLaren Vale

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin medium plus to high and dusty, alcohol medium to medium plus, body medium to medium plus, fullest in Brunello.

home.home: Tuscany: the hills of Chianti Classico, Montalcino, where it is called Brunello, and Montepulciano, where it is Prugnolo Gentile, with the Maremma as Morellino. Brunello is Sangiovese alone; Chianti Classico needs at least 80 per cent. Romagna, Umbria and the Marche grow it too.
home.abroad: Corsica calls it Nielluccio, the grape of Patrimonio. California, Washington and McLaren Vale in South Australia bottle a little; these tend to be riper and rounder, with less of the sour cherry snap.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius for Chianti; Brunello a degree or two warmer.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, tall enough for the cherry and herb scent to gather.
service.decant: Rarely for a young Chianti; consider it for a young Brunello after a taste, or an old one with sediment.
service.age: Most Chianti within five years, Riserva longer; Brunello five to twenty.

with.dish: Pasta in a slow cooked meat ragù

labels.means: The historic heart between Florence and Siena, its own DOCG under the black rooster: at least 80 per cent Sangiovese.
Sangiovese alone from Montalcino, at least two years in oak and released years after the harvest.
Sangiovese, there called Prugnolo Gentile, from the Tuscan town; nothing to do with the Montepulciano grape.
A trade name, not a law: Tuscan reds outside the old rules, often Sangiovese with Cabernet or Merlot.

guest.a: No, a place. Chianti and Chianti Classico are Tuscan zones, and the grape in both is mostly Sangiovese; Classico must hold at least 80 per cent.

guest.q: Why does this red taste so tart on its own?
guest.a: Sangiovese keeps high acidity. Alone it can feel sharp, but beside tomato, olive oil or a fatty cut the tartness reads as freshness, which is why Tuscany drinks it with food.

guest.q: What makes Brunello different from Chianti?
guest.a: Brunello is Sangiovese alone from the warmer hill of Montalcino, with at least two years in oak and a long wait before release: fuller, firmer and longer lived.

compare.tell: Nebbiolo is paler, with tar and rose petal and a far bigger, more drying grip; Sangiovese is a little deeper, with tomato leaf and dried oregano.
Tempranillo from Rioja swaps tomato leaf for dill and coconut from American oak, with softer acidity; Sangiovese is tarter and more savoury.
Montepulciano is deeper in colour and darker in fruit, black cherry and black plum, with softer acidity; Sangiovese is paler and tarter, with tomato leaf.

cards.front: Sangiovese: its local names in Montalcino, Montepulciano, Scansano and Corsica?
cards.back: Brunello in Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile in Montepulciano, Morellino in Scansano and Nielluccio in Corsica.

cards.front: Sangiovese blind: which two notes and which structure give it away?
cards.back: Sour cherry and tomato leaf, on high acidity and a dusty, firm tannin, with a medium body and often an orange rim early.

cards.front: Sangiovese: the minimum in Chianti Classico, Vino Nobile and Brunello?
cards.back: Chianti Classico at least 80 per cent, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano at least 70, Brunello di Montalcino 100 per cent.

questions.q: A red poured blind is medium ruby with an orange rim: sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano, high acidity and a dusty, firm tannin. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Sour cherry and tomato leaf on high acidity and dusty tannin are Sangiovese. Nebbiolo, the nearest wrong option, would be paler, with tar and roses and a bigger grip.

questions.q: A guest orders Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and asks whether it is made from the grape of the same name. Which grape leads it?
questions.exp: Vino Nobile is named for the Tuscan town and is at least 70 per cent Sangiovese, there called Prugnolo Gentile. The Montepulciano grape, the nearest wrong option, belongs to Abruzzo and the Adriatic side.

questions.q: A table orders pasta in a long cooked tomato and meat ragù and asks for a red that will not taste flat beside the tomato. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Tomato is high in acid, and a red with less acidity tastes flat beside it. Chianti Classico keeps Sangiovese's high acidity; the Merlot, the nearest wrong option, is softer and lower in acid.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. Nothing contradicts TASTE.world old.

The Tuscan rules (Chianti Classico at least 80 per cent, Vino Nobile at least 70, Brunello 100 per cent with two years in oak and a delayed release), the local names Brunello, Prugnolo Gentile, Morellino and Nielluccio, Patrimonio, and the first commercial Sangiovese of McLaren Vale in 1985 all stand on the Codex's own Tuscany, Corsica and McLaren Vale records.

The parents, Ciliegiolo and Calabrese di Montenuovo, a little known vine from Campania found on Montenuovo near Naples, stand on the Vitis paper (primary) and an encyclopedia entry. The year is left out: sources give 2004 for the finding of the vines and 2007 for the paper. Another Italian study of the same years read the relation the other way, Sangiovese as a parent of Ciliegiolo, so the line says DNA work suggests and not shows.
The name said to come from sanguis Jovis, the blood of Jupiter, is left out: every source calls it a legend and none could be confirmed beyond trade writing.

Abroad, riper and rounder for California, Washington and McLaren Vale stands on Wine Australia's page for the Australian side and on trade writing for California whose authors are living and cannot be cited; a checker should weigh the hedge.
INTRO_GRAPES gives Sangiovese tannin 3 where TASTE gives 2 and GRAPES says medium plus to high; the structure line follows GRAPES and the grid (medium plus to high, dusty).

The ladder takes two rungs, moderate and warm: the Court's grid reads Chianti Classico and Brunello as moderate, and INTRO_GRAPES calls the grape moderate to warm. The warm rung places the Maremma at Scansano; the Codex Tuscany record warns against assuming every Morellino is soft, so the rung says riper, not softer.
